config.title: Berlin Sauna Guide - FAQ
config.subtitle: What a Berlin sauna costs for the length of stay you actually have, what you are expected to take off, and which venues are open this month.

items.q: Do you have to be naked in a Berlin sauna?
items.a: **In the sauna itself, yes.** The Berliner Bäder-Betriebe house rules put it in plain English: the sauna areas are textile-free zones and **may only be used naked**, and you must sit or lie on a towel big enough to cover the wood. Private venues follow the same standard. What differs is how far the rule reaches. **vabali spa Berlin is textile free in the entire building** and asks you not to wear swimwear at any time, including in the restaurant. **Liquidrom, Stadtbad Oderberger and the public baths** want standard swimwear in the water and nothing in the hot room. There is no venue where you keep a swimsuit on in the sauna, so if that is a hard no, book a pool-only ticket instead.

items.q: What does a sauna cost in Berlin?
items.a: **Between about 20 and 57 euros, and the length of your stay decides which venue is cheapest.** Liquidrom sells 90 minutes for **22.00 euros**, two hours for **24.50** and three hours for **29.50**, with the sauna area adding **2.50** and each further 30 minutes adding **5.00**. vabali sells **27.50 euros** for two hours on a weekday, **36.50** for four, **45.50** for six and **51.50** for a day pass, each 3 to 5 euros more at the weekend. Stadtbad Oderberger sells a fixed two hour swim-and-sauna slot for roughly **20 to 22 euros**. The public pool saunas are the cheapest at 13 to 23 euros, but they are closed until 1 November 2026.

**It depends entirely on how long you stay, and the lines cross at about three and a half hours.** Up to roughly three hours **Liquidrom** wins: two hours with the sauna is 27.00 euros against vabali's 27.50, and three hours is 32.00 against vabali's 36.50. From about three and a half hours **vabali** takes over, because Liquidrom keeps charging 5.00 euros for every extra half hour while vabali's blocks get wider. At six hours vabali is 45.50 and Liquidrom is 62.00. At eight hours the day pass at 51.50 is barely more than half what Liquidrom would charge.

items.q: Are Berlin public swimming pool saunas open in summer?
items.a: **No. Every Berliner Bäder-Betriebe sauna is closed for the whole summer season and reopens on 1 November 2026.** That is the operator's own published date. It matters because these are the cheap ones: a three hour sauna ticket is **13.00 euros** in the cheapest category and **20.00 euros** at Stadtbad Neukölln, with day tickets at 15.00 to 23.00. Two extra details for when they reopen: the sauna ticket is sold **at the counter only**, with no online sale, and you need a **refundable 10 euro deposit** for the sauna chip. The sauna ticket also covers the swimming hall if there is capacity.

items.q: Do I need to book a Berlin sauna in advance?
items.a: **Only at Stadtbad Oderberger, where it is unavoidable.** Non-hotel guests book a **fixed two hour slot online**, and the sauna is only bookable from 11:00 at the earliest. The slot does not extend, last entry is 30 minutes before it ends, and leaving late costs 10 euros per 30 minutes. Opening times are published every Friday for the following two weeks and the pool closes entirely on event days, so check the calendar in that window. Liquidrom asks you to reserve a time slot but sells on the day. vabali does not need a booking for normal admission.

items.q: How old do you have to be to visit a Berlin sauna?
items.a: **It varies more than you would expect, from 12 to 18.** vabali admits children **from 12**, and everyone under 18 needs a legal guardian with them. Liquidrom is **14 plus**, with 14 to 17 year olds accompanied by a parent or legal guardian. Stadtbad Oderberger's sauna is **18 plus only**, although under 16s can swim with an adult. In the public baths, children under 14 are only allowed into the sauna with an adult. If you are travelling with teenagers, check the specific venue before you plan the afternoon.

items.q: What should I take to a sauna in Berlin?
items.a: **Two towels, flip flops, and swimwear unless you are going to vabali.** One towel is compulsory to sit or lie on inside the sauna at every venue, so you need a second one to dry with. Liquidrom rents two towels for 9.00 euros and a bathrobe with a sauna towel for 14.00. **vabali requires a bathrobe or kimono and bathing shoes outside the water**, and does not allow swimwear anywhere. Bring **cash for Stadtbad Oderberger**: the key card deposit is 20 euros and they only accept notes up to 20, with no deposit meaning no entry. Liquidrom is entirely cashless and does not allow phones in the spa areas.

items.q: Is Thermen am Europa-Center still open?
items.a: **No. It closed in 2020 and has not reopened.** The rooftop bath at Nürnberger Straße 7 off Kurfürstendamm shut during the pandemic, the operating company became insolvent, the lease ended, and its old website no longer resolves. Plenty of directory and listing sites still show it with opening hours and prices, which is a good reason to check an operator's own page before you cross the city for a sauna.

items.q: When is the best time of day to go to a sauna in Berlin?
items.a: **Late afternoon or early evening, after the walking is done.** Heat before a day of sightseeing leaves you flat, and every one of these venues is open late: Liquidrom until midnight and until 01:00 on Friday and Saturday, vabali until midnight all year. If you have joined my free walking tour, it finishes at Hackescher Markt around lunchtime, which puts you about 15 minutes from Oderberger Straße on the U8 and M1 and about 20 minutes from Liquidrom. Weekdays are also cheaper at vabali and quieter everywhere.
